assessment.rationale: Materially relevant because it focuses on what can be claimed safely before a stable boundary exists, but its center of gravity is kernel/runtime porting rather than app-side semantics. It is strongest on provisional-versus-stable discipline and layer separation, and weakest on app-level claim wording, authoritative boundary identity, and wire-auditable interop evidence.
strengths: Strong provisional-versus-blocked framing helps avoid freezing draft behavior as a final contract.
Explicit substrate/feed/group/CAS/app boundary language helps separate local shortcuts from protocol-boundary claims.
Connects early conformance to frozen binding/session/message specs instead of a monolithic harness clone.
weaknesses: Does not define an app-side B-side partial-conformance claim format.
Leaves authoritative protocol-boundary identity underdefined when local IDs remain internal.
Provides little concrete evidence shape for Bob or Carol to audit claims from observed wire artifacts.
risks: Porting-boundary guidance could be misread as an endorsement of incomplete app-contract claims.
Provisional signature-carriage language could harden into an accidental interoperability requirement.
Open capability, witness, and authority semantics leave room for Mallory-benefiting ambiguity.
open_questions: Should app partial-conformance profiles be distinct from kernel/runtime port claims?
Which identity is authoritative at the protocol boundary for first-slice apps that still use local IDs internally?
What minimum app-semantics set is safe to claim now, and what must stay blocked pending DR-tuhaz and DR-davod?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.
